Sample size calculation for ordinal outcomes: artcatr

Source: vignettes/artcatr.Rmd
artcatr.Rmd
library(artcatr)

Overview

artcatr calculates sample size and power for a two-arm randomized trial with an ordered categorical outcome, analysed by a proportional-odds model. It uses the ologit method of White, Marley-Zagar, Morris, Parmar, Royston & Babiker (2023). This packages implements the Stata functions (artcat, White et al. (2023)) into R (artcatr). artcatr requires that the most-right level probabilities need to be specified, that is, the input vectors pc (or pe) need to sum up to one.

The examples below reproduce the worked examples from White et al. (2023).

Favourable and unfavourable outcomes

Outcome levels are always supplied in increasing order (level 1, 2, …, K), but that ordering says nothing about which end of the scale represents a good outcome. White et al (2023) therefore introduce a favourable option: favourable = TRUE means level 1 (the left-most level) is the most favourable outcome and level K is the least favourable, and vice versa.

favourable determines how a margin (expressed as an odds ratio for the null hypothesis) is interpreted, i.e. whether the design is a superiority, non-inferiority, or substantial-superiority trial (that is, a superiority trial showing that the treatment is substantially - by a margin - superior than control). Following White et al (2023, sec. 3), artcatr() classifies the trial as follows:

margin favourable Trial type
= 1 either superiority
< 1 TRUE non-inferiority
< 1 FALSE substantial-superiority
> 1 TRUE substantial-superiority
> 1 FALSE non-inferiority

If favourable is left as NULL (the default), artcatr() infers the direction from whether the anticipated average odds ratio lies above or below margin, and flags the result as (inferred) in the printed summary. It is good practice, however, to set favourable explicitly based on clinical knowledge of the outcome scale, rather than relying on inference from the anticipated effect size:

artcatr(pc = c(.018, .036, .156, .141, .39, .259), 
       or = 1 / 1.77, 
       power = .8)
#> artcatr: sample size for an ordered categorical outcome (proportional-odds model)
#> 
#>       based on the Stata implementation from White et al. (2023)----------------------------------------------------------------------
#> Type of trial                         superiority
#> Favourable/unfavourable outcome       unfavourable  (inferred)
#> Null hypothesis                       odds ratio = 1
#> Superiority region                    odds ratio < 1
#> Allocation ratio C:E                  1:1
#> Anticipated probabilities, control    0.018 0.036 0.156 0.141 0.390 0.259
#>                       experimental    given by odds ratio = 0.565
#> 
#> Table of anticipated probabilities
#>                                C       E
#> 1   least favourable       0.018   0.010
#> 2                          0.036   0.021
#> 3                          0.156   0.099
#> 4                          0.141   0.103
#> 5                          0.390   0.384
#> 6   most favourable        0.259   0.382
#> 
#> Alpha                                 0.05 (two-sided)
#> Power (designed)                      0.8
#> Method                                ologit (variance NA)
#> 
#> Total sample size (calculated)        322
#> Sample size per group (calculated)    161 161
#> ----------------------------------------------------------------------

Examples

The following examples reproduces the results from White et al. (2023).

A six-level ordered outcome

The FLU-IVIG trial (Davey et al 2019) had a six-level ordinal outcome. Anticipated control-arm probabilities are given via pc, one per level including the right-most, and the anticipated treatment effect via a common odds ratio or. Here the left-most level is the least favourable outcome, so favourable = FALSE.

By default artcatr() uses the new ologit method (with variance = "NA"):

artcatr(pc = c(.018, .036, .156, .141, .39, .259), 
       or = 1 / 1.77, 
       power = .8,
       favourable = FALSE)
#> artcatr: sample size for an ordered categorical outcome (proportional-odds model)
#> 
#>       based on the Stata implementation from White et al. (2023)----------------------------------------------------------------------
#> Type of trial                         superiority
#> Favourable/unfavourable outcome       unfavourable
#> Null hypothesis                       odds ratio = 1
#> Superiority region                    odds ratio < 1
#> Allocation ratio C:E                  1:1
#> Anticipated probabilities, control    0.018 0.036 0.156 0.141 0.390 0.259
#>                       experimental    given by odds ratio = 0.565
#> 
#> Table of anticipated probabilities
#>                                C       E
#> 1   least favourable       0.018   0.010
#> 2                          0.036   0.021
#> 3                          0.156   0.099
#> 4                          0.141   0.103
#> 5                          0.390   0.384
#> 6   most favourable        0.259   0.382
#> 
#> Alpha                                 0.05 (two-sided)
#> Power (designed)                      0.8
#> Method                                ologit (variance NA)
#> 
#> Total sample size (calculated)        322
#> Sample size per group (calculated)    161 161
#> ----------------------------------------------------------------------

This matches the sample size (n = 322, 161 per arm) reported by White et al (2023).

Comparison with Whitehead’s method

Whitehead’s (1993) original method is available via method = "whitehead", for comparison with the newer ologit method:

artcatr(pc = c(.018, .036, .156, .141, .39, .259), 
       or = 1 / 1.77, 
       power = .8,
       favourable = FALSE, 
       method = "whitehead")
#> artcatr: sample size for an ordered categorical outcome (proportional-odds model)
#> 
#>       based on the Stata implementation from White et al. (2023)----------------------------------------------------------------------
#> Type of trial                         superiority
#> Favourable/unfavourable outcome       unfavourable
#> Null hypothesis                       odds ratio = 1
#> Superiority region                    odds ratio < 1
#> Allocation ratio C:E                  1:1
#> Anticipated probabilities, control    0.018 0.036 0.156 0.141 0.390 0.259
#>                       experimental    given by odds ratio = 0.565
#> 
#> Table of anticipated probabilities
#>                                C       E
#> 1   least favourable       0.018   0.010
#> 2                          0.036   0.021
#> 3                          0.156   0.099
#> 4                          0.141   0.103
#> 5                          0.390   0.384
#> 6   most favourable        0.259   0.382
#> 
#> Alpha                                 0.05 (two-sided)
#> Power (designed)                      0.8
#> Method                                Whitehead
#> 
#> Total sample size (calculated)        320
#> Sample size per group (calculated)    160 160
#> ----------------------------------------------------------------------

Here Whitehead’s method gives a slightly smaller sample size (n = 320) than the default ologit method (n = 322).

Comparison with psamsize from Hmisc

Whitehead’s (1993) method is implemented in the psamsize function in the ‘Hmisc’ package. The small difference to the artcatr Whitehead option is due to ceiling of numbers.

pc <- c(.018, .036, .156, .141, .39, .259)
or <- 1 / 1.77
pe <- or * cumsum(pc) / (1 - cumsum(pc) + or * cumsum(pc))
pe <- diff(c(0, pe))
pbar <- (pc + pe) / 2

Hmisc::posamsize(p = pbar,
                 odds.ratio = or,
                 alpha = 0.05,
                 power = 0.8)
#> Total sample size: 319.2 
#> Efficiency of design compared with continuous response: 0.905

Non-inferiority trials

A non-inferiority trial is specified via margin, expressed as an odds ratio defining the null hypothesis. Here the anticipated odds ratio is or = 1 (no average treatment effect), and the non-inferiority margin is an odds ratio of 1.33:

artcatr(pc = c(.010, .021, .099, .103, .384, .383), 
       or = 1, 
       margin = 1.33,
       power = .8, 
       favourable = FALSE)
#> artcatr: sample size for an ordered categorical outcome (proportional-odds model)
#> 
#>       based on the Stata implementation from White et al. (2023)----------------------------------------------------------------------
#> Type of trial                         non-inferiority
#> Favourable/unfavourable outcome       unfavourable
#> Null hypothesis                       odds ratio = 1.33
#> Non-inferiority region                odds ratio < 1.33
#> Allocation ratio C:E                  1:1
#> Anticipated probabilities, control    0.010 0.021 0.099 0.103 0.384 0.383
#>                       experimental    given by odds ratio = 1
#> 
#> Table of anticipated probabilities
#>                                C       E    E null
#> 1   least favourable       0.010   0.010     0.013
#> 2                          0.021   0.021     0.028
#> 3                          0.099   0.099     0.125
#> 4                          0.103   0.103     0.122
#> 5                          0.384   0.384     0.394
#> 6   most favourable        0.383   0.383     0.318
#> 
#> Alpha                                 0.05 (two-sided)
#> Power (designed)                      0.8
#> Method                                ologit (variance NA)
#> 
#> Total sample size (calculated)        1314
#> Sample size per group (calculated)    657 657
#> ----------------------------------------------------------------------

Non-proportional odds

Long et al. (2025) highlights that it is not relevant that the proportional odds assumption holds for testing the null hypothesis of no treatment effect. artcatr also allows for non-proportional odds by specifying pe and pc directly instead of a common odds ratio.

artcatr(pc = c(.010, .021, .099, .103, .384, .383), 
       pe = c(.020, .021, .099, .103, .384, .373), 
       power = .9, 
       favourable = FALSE)
#> artcatr: sample size for an ordered categorical outcome (proportional-odds model)
#> 
#>       based on the Stata implementation from White et al. (2023)----------------------------------------------------------------------
#> Type of trial                         superiority
#> Favourable/unfavourable outcome       unfavourable
#> Null hypothesis                       odds ratio = 1
#> Superiority region                    odds ratio < 1
#> Allocation ratio C:E                  1:1
#> Anticipated probabilities, control    0.010 0.021 0.099 0.103 0.384 0.383
#>                       experimental    0.020 0.021 0.099 0.103 0.384 0.373
#> Anticipated average odds ratio        1.056
#> 
#> Table of anticipated probabilities
#>                                C       E
#> 1   least favourable       0.010   0.020
#> 2                          0.021   0.021
#> 3                          0.099   0.099
#> 4                          0.103   0.103
#> 5                          0.384   0.384
#> 6   most favourable        0.383   0.373
#> 
#> Alpha                                 0.05 (two-sided)
#> Power (designed)                      0.9
#> Method                                ologit (variance NA)
#> 
#> Total sample size (calculated)        48130
#> Sample size per group (calculated)    24065 24065
#> ----------------------------------------------------------------------

Cumulative probabilities

Anticipated probabilities may instead be specified as cumulative probabilities (cumulative = TRUE), which can be more natural when the outcome levels are thresholds on an underlying scale.

A three-level outcome:

artcatr(pc = c(.01, .4, 1), 
       cumulative = TRUE, 
       or = .375, 
       power = .9,
       favourable = FALSE)
#> artcatr: sample size for an ordered categorical outcome (proportional-odds model)
#> 
#>       based on the Stata implementation from White et al. (2023)----------------------------------------------------------------------
#> Type of trial                         superiority
#> Favourable/unfavourable outcome       unfavourable
#> Null hypothesis                       odds ratio = 1
#> Superiority region                    odds ratio < 1
#> Allocation ratio C:E                  1:1
#> Anticipated probabilities, control    0.01 0.40 1.00 (cumulative)
#>                       experimental    given by odds ratio = 0.375
#> 
#> Table of anticipated probabilities
#>                                C       E
#> 1   least favourable       0.010   0.004
#> 2                          0.390   0.196
#> 3   most favourable        0.600   0.800
#> 
#> Alpha                                 0.05 (two-sided)
#> Power (designed)                      0.9
#> Method                                ologit (variance NA)
#> 
#> Total sample size (calculated)        216
#> Sample size per group (calculated)    108 108
#> ----------------------------------------------------------------------

A four-level outcome:

artcatr(pc = c(.01, .1, .4, 1),

       favourable = FALSE)
#> artcatr: sample size for an ordered categorical outcome (proportional-odds model)
#>

#> Null hypothesis                       odds ratio = 1

#>                       experimental    given by odds ratio = 0.375

#> 3                          0.300   0.160

#> 
#> Alpha                                 0.05 (two-sided)
#> Power (designed)                      0.9

#> 
#> Total sample size (calculated)        212
#> Sample size per group (calculated)    106 106
#> ----------------------------------------------------------------------

A three-level outcome with a different split of probability across levels:

artcatr(pc = c(.4, .7, 1), 
       cumulative = TRUE, 
       or = .375, 
       power = .9,
       favourable = FALSE)
#> artcatr: sample size for an ordered categorical outcome (proportional-odds model)
#>

Working with the results

artcatr() returns (invisibly) a list of class "artcatr", containing the computed sample size (or power), the anticipated probability table, and other design parameters. Use summary() for a tidy version of the probability table:

fit <- artcatr(pc = c(.018, .036, .156, .141, .39, .259), 
              or = 1 / 1.77, 
              power = .8,
              favourable = FALSE, 
              quiet = TRUE)
summary(fit)
#> Design: superiority (unfavourable outcome; method = ologit, variance = NA)
#> Sample size (calculated): 322 total (C = 161, E = 161), power (designed) = 0.800
#> 
#>  level      description control experimental
#>      1 least favourable   0.018        0.010
#>      2                    0.036        0.021
#>      3                    0.156        0.099
#>      4                    0.141        0.103
#>      5                    0.390        0.384
#>      6  most favourable   0.259        0.382

References

White IR, Marley-Zagar E, Morris TP, Parmar MKB, Royston P, Babiker AG (2023). artcat: Sample-size calculation for an ordered categorical outcome. Stata Journal 23(1):3-23. doi:10.1177/1536867X231161934

Whitehead J (1993). Sample size calculations for ordered categorical data. Statistics in Medicine 12:2257-2271.

Davey RT Jr, Fernandez-Cruz E, Markowitz N, et al (2019). Anti-influenza hyperimmune intravenous immunoglobulin for adults with influenza A or B infection (FLU-IVIG): a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet Respiratory Medicine 7(11):951-963.

Long Y, Wiegers EJA, Jacobs BC, Steyerberg EW, van Zwet EW (2025). Role of the proportional odds assumption for the analysis of ordinal outcomes in neurologic trials. Neurology 105(8):e214146. doi:10.1212/WNL.0000000000214146
